To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

photo-oxidation of organic matter in the surface layer is a major sink of oxygen in all marine regions, that this process is driven by ultraviolet light and is therefore only possible in regions where the upper layer of seawater is vertically stratified, that photochemical oxygen loss is a seasonal process in the temperate zone, and that the balance between oxygen production and loss is the reason for the constancy of oxygen concentrations in the tropical and subtropical oceans.

(1) photochemical oxygen consumption is the largest sink for oxygen at the surface of oceans and seas; (2) the oxygen demand is of the same magnitude as the oxygen production by photosynthesis; (3) oxygen production and loss are in balance in the ocean surface layers of the tropics and sub-tropics; (4) the oxygen concentration in the ocean surface waters is constant; and (5) the oxygen budget is not closed in the temperate zone.
the oxygen demand of photochemistry and that of heterotrophic activity are of the same order, and that both are of the same magnitude as the oxygen production of photosynthesis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question whether the oxygen concentration in seawater at the ocean surface is a result of the balance between oxygen loss due to photooxidation and oxygen gain through photosynthesis.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
photochemical processes in seawater are the major sink of oxygen in marine surface layers.

the oxygen concentration in the surface ocean is determined mainly by the balance between photosynthesis and respiration, but that in some regions and seasons photochemical oxygen demand is a significant contributor to the total oxygen loss in the ocean surface.

oxygen in the surface waters of the world's seas and oceans is in dynamic equilibrium between oxygen production and oxygen loss, the latter being due to the activity of photochemical and microheterotrophic processes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ocean surface layer, where the bulk of the photosynthetic oxygen is produced, is also the layer where most of this oxygen is lost.

the photochemical oxygen demand in the upper layer of the ocean is of the same magnitude as the oxygen released by photosynthetic processes, so the net flux of oxygen across the sea-air interface is close to zero.
the oxygen budget of the surface layer of the world's sea is in balance.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the oxygen balance of the world's seas and oceans is a function of the vertical stratification of the surface layer and that the oxygen concentration in the upper layer is not a reliable indicator of oxygen production or consumption in the water column below.
photochemical processes in surface seawater are not just an interesting laboratory curiosity but a process that is of the same importance as primary production in the marine carbon cycle.
oxygen loss in the upper layers of the ocean is not restricted to the photic zone but is a surface phenomenon that is driven by ultraviolet light.
